extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students working through textbook exercises (proofs, functions, number theory, set theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and checking elementary undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (functions, relations, modular arithmetic, irrationality, inequalities, induction, continuity). Emphasis on standard proof techniques and verifying properties like injective/surjective/bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove injectivity by f(a)=f(b) ⇒ a=b
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that f is injective, assume f(a) = f(b) for arbitrary domain elements and deduce a = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern: start with f(a)=f(b), use the function definition (parity, prime factorization, algebraic manipulation) to force equality of components. Example: for f(a,b)=2^{a-1}(2b-1), equate factors and use odd/even parity to get a=c and b=d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove surjectivity by constructing preimage for arbitrary y
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f is surjective, fix y in the codomain and explicitly produce x in the domain with f(x)=y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: use unique prime factorization to split y into required factors (example: write n=2^{k-1}(2ℓ−1)); solve algebraically for x; demonstrate domain membership of constructed preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove bijectivity by proving injective and surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Show f is bijective by proving both injectivity and surjectivity (or by constructing a two-sided inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either separately prove injective and surjective as above, or produce a function g such that g◦f = id and f◦g = id. Examples: show g is left and right inverse of f to deduce bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive when direct implication is awkward
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove an implication P ⇒ Q by proving its contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P when that route is simpler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving 'f injective ⇒ LHS ⊆ RHS' is done by proving '(LHS ⊈ RHS) ⇒ f not injective' (contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired statement and derive a contradiction from established arithmetic/algebraic facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used widely: assume existence of integer satisfying incompatible congruences, assume rationality of known irrationals, assume maximum exists in set of rationals approximating √2. Follow algebra to reach impossibility (e.g., divisibility contradictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexample to disprove universal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal claim false, provide one explicit counterexample and check the claimed equality/property fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show image of intersection need not equal intersection of images by giving f and sets W,X where f(W∩X) ≠ f(W)∩f(X); show f(f^{-1}(Y)) ≠ Y via a non-surjective f and Y containing non-image elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show relation is equivalence: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a relation ℛ is an equivalence relation, verify reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity directly from the defining condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: relation on R^2 by (x,y) ℛ (s,t) iff x^2+y^2 = s^2+t^2 — check each property with algebraic equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define induced function on power sets and prove bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a bijection f:A→B define g:𝒫(A)→𝒫(B) by g(X)={f(x):x∈X} and show g is bijective by direct check of injectivity and surjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surjectivity: for Y⊆B, take X={x∈A: f(x)∈Y} and show g(X)=Y. Injectivity: if g(Z)=g(W) use injectivity of f to deduce Z=W.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show function on equivalence classes is well-defined
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining f on equivalence classes [(x)], verify that equal classes map to equal values: if [(x)]=[(s)] then f([(x)])=f([(s)]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define f([(x)]) = x mod n representative; show independence of representative using congruence properties and Euclidean division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Euclidean division to pick canonical representatives in Zn
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with Z_n, express any integer x = qn + r with r in {0,...,n−1} and use r as canonical representative to define functions or remainders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows well-definedness: if [x]=[y] then remainders coincide because n divides difference and remainders lie in restricted range, so equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit parity and uniqueness of prime factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use odd/even distinctions and unique prime factorization to deduce equality of exponents or components in multiplicative encodings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mapping (a,b)→2^{a-1}(2b−1) uses parity: 2-power factor forces exponent equality; unique factorization used to construct preimages by separating 2-adic part and odd part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equalities/inclusions with images and preimages characterize injective/surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Use set identities: X = f^{-1}(f(X)) for all X⊆A iff f is injective; Y = f(f^{-1}(Y)) for all Y⊆B iff f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove each direction: injective ⇒ equality via uniqueness; conversely use contrapositive by finding specific X or Y when not injective/surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use left/right inverses to establish bijectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function g is both a left and right inverse of f (g◦f = id and f◦g = id), then f is bijective and g = f^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate cases separately: check g(f(n))=n and f(g(n))=n via case analysis (e.g., parity of n) to validate inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity/surjectivity consequences for compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is injective and g◦f = g◦h then f = h. If g is surjective and f◦g = h◦g then f = h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: apply injectivity/surjectivity at appropriate points (apply g to f(x) and h(x), or find y with g(y)=x) to deduce equality for all x.

rubrics_metrics.name: If f◦f bijective then f bijective; likewise if f◦f◦f = id then f bijective
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition power of f being bijective (or equal to the identity) implies f itself is bijective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: injectivity and surjectivity of composition transfer back to f by algebraic manipulation (e.g., injectivity of f◦f forces f injective; surjectivity of f◦f gives preimages for f). If f^3 = id then f has inverse f^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: To show commutation constraints for all g, force fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f◦g)=(g◦f) must hold for every g, conclude strong restriction on f (e.g., f(x)=x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: plugging constant g_c forces f(c)=c for all c, hence f=id; check that f=id indeed satisfies the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check falsity of purported function identities with concrete x
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove functional equalities like f◦(g+h) = f◦g + f◦h provide a concrete counterexample x where the two sides differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples used: choose f(x)=x^2, g(x)=h(x)=x and evaluate at x=1 to show inequality; similarly for reciprocal/composition identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular arithmetic as non-existence certificate (choose modulus wisely)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show an integer equation has no integer solutions, reduce modulo n; a modulus with no solutions implies none exist over Z. But a solution modulo n does not imply integer solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 5y^2−4x^2=7 has no integer solution by working mod 4; warning: picking a 'bad' modulus may give false positives (solutions mod n even when none over Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove irrationality by parity/divisibility contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a purported rational expression for a known irrational, clear denominators, and derive divisibility contradiction (both numerator and denominator divisible by prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: √6 irrational; ³√25 irrational: show prime divides both numerator and denominator contradiction with gcd=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show rational k-th root must be integer if not introducing common factors
rubrics_metrics.description: If k-th root of integer k is rational, show denominator must divide numerator leading to denominator=1, hence integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: write k = a^k / b^k, deduce b divides a, use gcd=1 to conclude b=1; used to show certain k-th roots are integer only when trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Bézout/gcd arguments to force integer conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When rationality assumptions produce gcd constraints, use Bézout's identity to derive divisibility relations that force denominators to be ±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if √k is rational then kb^2 = a^2; combine with ax+by=1 to show b divides a and so b=1 contradicting non-integer assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction for parity/power properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Use induction to prove multiplicative properties for all natural numbers (e.g., 5^k is odd for all k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case k=1 trivial; induction step: product of odd numbers is odd, conclude for all k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove inequalities using squares and non-negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive inequalities by noting (x−y)^2 ≥ 0 or similar squares, expand and rearrange to obtain desired inequality (e.g., x/y + y/x ≥ 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard route: expand (x−y)^2, rearrange and divide by positive quantities when permitted; treat equality cases separately (x=y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Intermediate Value Theorem to deduce monotonicity from bijectivity+continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous bijection f:R→R must be strictly monotone; if not monotone there are x1<x2<x3 where f increases then decreases (or vice versa), and IVT produces distinct points mapping to same value, contradicting injectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break into cases comparing f(x1),f(x2),f(x3), apply IVT on appropriate interval to find distinct preimages of same value; similar symmetric treatment for decrease-then-increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic manipulation to derive explicit inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve equation y=f(x) for x algebraically to obtain closed-form f^{-1}(y); verify by substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: invert f(x) = (x+1)/(x+2) by solving for x in terms of y to get f^{-1}(y) = (2y−1)/(1−y), and check domain exclusions.
